title: Trilce: Poem XXXII - 999 Calories
text:
999 calories

Rumbbb...Trrrapprrr rrach...chaz

Serpentine u of the pastry-maker

giraffed toward the eardrum.


Who like the ices. But no.

Who like what goes neither more nor less.

Who like the golden mean.


1,000 calories.

The gringo firmament blues and laughs

its great composure. Down comes

the turkey-proud sun and stirs up the hooves

of the coldest one.


It mimics the cuckoo: Roooooooeeeis...

tender autorail, mobile of thirst,

running as far as the beach.


Air, air! Ice!

If at least the heat (__________ Better

                                   I say nothing.


And even the very pen

with which I write finally snaps.


Thirty-three trillion three hundred thirty

and three calories.
editorial_note: The translation preserves Vallejo's sound effects, invented forms, numerical escalation, and broken aside.

title: Trilce: Poem XV - In That Corner Where We Slept Together
text:
In that corner where we slept together

so many nights, now I have sat down

to walk. The bed of the dead bride and groom

was taken away, or perhaps who knows what happened.


You came early on other business,

and now you are not here. It is the corner

where beside you, one night, I read,

among your tender points,

a tale by Daudet. It is the beloved

corner. Do not mistake it.


I have begun remembering the vanished

summer days, your coming and going,

scant and full and pale through the rooms.


On this rainy night,

now far from both of us two, I suddenly leap...

There are two doors opening closing,

two doors that go and come in the wind,

shadow                      to                      shadow.
editorial_note: The translation keeps the impossible action of sitting down to walk and the final spaced shadow-to-shadow doors.

title: Trilce: Poem XXXIII - If It Rained Tonight, I Would Withdraw
text:
If it rained tonight, I would withdraw

from here a thousand years.

Better just a hundred.

As if nothing had happened, I would make

the account that I am still coming.


Or without mother, without beloved, without obstinacy

to bend down and peer at the bottom, by sheer

pulse,

this night like this, I would be combing out

the Vedic fiber,

the Vedic wool of my final end, thread

of the devil, trace of having had

by the noses

two discordant clappers of time

                    in one same bell.


Make the account of my life

or make the account of my not yet having been born;

I will not manage to free myself.


It will not be what has not yet come, but

what has arrived and already gone,

but what has arrived and already gone.
editorial_note: The translation preserves the impossible arithmetic of time, birth, withdrawal, and the double bell-clapper.

title: Beloved, Tonight You Have Crucified Yourself...
text:
Beloved, tonight you have crucified yourself

upon the two curved beams of my kiss;

and your sorrow has told me that Jesus has wept,

and that there is a Good Friday sweeter than that kiss.


On this clear night when you have looked at me so much,

Death has been joyful and has sung in its bone.

On this September night there has been officiated

my second fall and the most human kiss.


Beloved, we will die together, the two of us, very close;

our lofty bitterness will slowly dry away;

and our dead lips will have touched shadow.


And there will be no more reproaches in your blessed eyes;

nor will I offend you again. And in one grave

the two of us will fall asleep, like two little siblings.
editorial_note: The translation keeps this variant's blessed eyes and religious-erotic imagery of kiss, fall, and shared grave.

title: The Poet to His Beloved
text:
Beloved: tonight you have crucified yourself

upon the two curved beams of my kiss;

and your sorrow has told me that Jesus has wept,

and that there is a Good Friday sweeter than that kiss.


Beloved: on this night when I have looked at you so much,

Death has been joyful and has sung in its bone.

On this September night there has been officiated

my second fall and the most human kiss.


Beloved, we will die together, the two of us, very close;

our lofty bitterness will slowly dry away;

and our dead lips will have touched shadow.


And there will be no more reproaches in your little green eyes,

nor will I offend you again. And in one grave

the two of us will fall asleep, like two little siblings.
editorial_note: The translation keeps this named variant's colon punctuation and 'little green eyes' distinct from the related text.
